pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 🧩 **Strand 4 — Computational Thinking**
Sub-strand 3: Robotics

Robots build cars, assist surgeons, explore Mars and even vacuum floors. In this unit you will review how robots are used in society and weigh up the benefits and challenges of using them.

pages.title: Applications of Robots in Society
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.4.3.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- define a robot;
- state the applications and uses of robots;
- explore the prospects and challenges of using robots.
A **robot** is a programmable machine that can **sense** its environment, **process** information and **act** to carry out tasks automatically, with little or no human help. **Robotics** is the branch of technology that deals with designing, building, programming and using robots.
| **Area** | **How robots are used** |
|---|---|
| Manufacturing | Robotic arms weld, paint and assemble cars and electronics; mass production of consumer and industrial goods |
| Assembling and packing | Robots pick, sort and pack goods in factories and warehouses (e.g. drinks bottling lines) |
| Health and surgery | Surgical robots (e.g. the da Vinci system) help surgeons make very precise cuts; robots deliver medicines in hospitals; robotic prosthetic limbs |
| Transport and delivery | Self-driving vehicles, autopilots; **drones** deliver medical supplies; in Ghana, **Zipline** drones have delivered blood and vaccines to health facilities since 2019 |
| Education | Educational robots (mBot, LEGO Mindstorms/Spike, micro:bit robots) teach programming |
| Laboratory research | Robots handle dangerous chemicals and test thousands of samples |
| Exploration | Mars rovers (Perseverance), underwater robots, robots that inspect pipelines and mines |
| Security and defence | Bomb-disposal robots; surveillance drones |
| Agriculture | Drones spray crops and photograph farms; robotic harvesters |
| Photography and media | Camera drones take aerial pictures and videos of events and landscapes |
| Home | Robot vacuum cleaners, lawn mowers, smart assistants |

pages.title: Prospects (benefits) and challenges of robots
pages.body:
## Prospects (benefits) and challenges of robots
| **Prospects / benefits** | **Challenges / disadvantages** |
|---|---|
| Work 24 hours without tiredness | Expensive to buy, program and maintain |
| High speed, precision and consistency | May replace some human jobs, causing unemployment |
| Do dangerous, dirty or boring work (e.g. mining, bomb disposal) | Need skilled engineers and reliable electricity |
| Reduce human error and improve quality | Cannot easily handle unexpected situations; limited creativity and emotion |
| Create new jobs in robot design, programming and repair | Faults or hacking can cause accidents |
| Reach places humans cannot (space, deep sea) | Ethical questions, e.g. responsibility when a robot causes harm |
> 🇬🇭 **Ghana connection** Ghanaian learners regularly compete in robotics competitions, and several organisations run robotics clubs and holiday camps for JHS and SHS learners. Ask your teacher whether your district runs a STEM or robotics programme.
> 🧪 **Activity — Debate**
“Robots will create more jobs than they destroy in Ghana.” Divide the class into two teams, research the prospects and challenges, and debate the motion.
